genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure answers calls from people in distress
early in her working life she raised the volume of her voice
that way of doing things drove callers to break off the exchange
she changed her way of speaking from top to bottom
she now leaves pauses and slows her delivery
she gives back the last word the caller has spoken
the caller's breathing ends up falling into step with hers
her colleagues have taken up the same method
she says this work has changed how she hears the people close to her
text: She speaks softly, the adviser on the helpline, and there is nothing accidental about it. When she started out, she lifted her voice to carry over the panic of the people ringing in. The effect baffled her. Callers stiffened, cut her off, put the phone down. So she turned the whole thing round. She leaves silences now, she slows down, she gives back the last word she has heard. As the breathing at the other end settles into step with her own, the strain eases without being named. She tells it plainly, with a shrug, as though anyone would have worked it out. Her colleagues took to copying her in earnest, because fewer of their calls were ending early. Then she adds something that makes her smile: the work has taught her to hear her own family, whom she thought she already knew.

units: the text passes judgement on an exhibition given over to the feelings
the first part of the route piles up video installations
that piling up wears out the attention of visitors
the feelings are handled there in a distant, teacherly way
the second part offers a space empty of any screen
there you listen to accounts of grief spoken by strangers
the public slows down there and shows feeling
the last stage invites you to set down on paper the feeling hardest to name
the critic advises walking the place in the other direction
text: You come away from this exhibition on the feelings with mixed impressions. The route through it is badly built at the start: room after room stacks screen upon screen, and the visitor, glutted, skims past everything. Anger, shame and delight get the same cool explanatory treatment, so that nothing in the visitor quickens. The designers seem to have grasped as much, since the second half puts a good deal of that right. A bare room, stripped of screens, asks you to listen to unknown voices telling of a grief; the quiet does the work on its own, and people soften, linger, double back on themselves. The last stage goes further still: you write on a card the feeling you find hardest to name, then post the card into a glass urn. The whole thing is worth the trip, so long as you walk it backwards.

units: the reader has asked a question about the kinship of two feelings
the writer describes fear as a pressure laid on the back of the neck
fear dampens the palms and cuts the breath short
sorrow is likened to a wet weight that covers you over
fear drives you to move whereas sorrow holds you still
both feelings slip away when you try to look at them head on
both grow quieter once you put them into words in front of someone
the writer explains in this way why he writes so often
the writer says he would rather have a clumsy sentence than advice
text: Your question has stayed with me since your letter came: is sorrow anything like fear? I turned it over at the window, and here is what I believe. Fear is a hand laid on the back of the neck. It grips, it presses, it wants you up and moving. It leaves the palms damp and the breath short. Sorrow presses nothing at all. It settles in, it lies on the chest like a soaked blanket, and it asks you to stop. One speeds you up, the other slows you down, and there lies the plainest difference between them. On one point, though, they are alike, and that point has occupied me since the cold months. Both slip away the moment you look straight at them, and both loosen their hold when you say them aloud to someone. That is why I write to you so often. Write back; your clumsiest sentence comforts me better than advice.

units: specialists draw a line between an emotion and a mood
three criteria hold that distinction up
an emotion is brief whereas a mood stretches much further
an emotion bears on a target you can point out
a mood has nobody it can be addressed to
the third criterion has to do with the traces left in the body
will alone does not call off the firing of an emotion
it can on the other hand shape the way that emotion shows
fear sends blood towards the muscles to make the body ready to act
text: Is an emotion, people often ask, really a different thing from a mood? Specialists say that it is, and they rest the case on three criteria. The first is duration: an emotion flares and dies away quickly, whereas a mood stretches over a far wider span. The second is the object: an emotion fastens on a target you can point to, while a mood drifts with nobody to receive it. The third is the mark left on the body, readable in the heartbeat, the sweat and the tightening of muscle. The next question is whether will alone can shut an emotion down. The answer is a qualified one: you shape the way it shows, you do not call off its firing. Last comes the use of fear. It readies the body to act by sending blood towards the muscles, which is why the hands clench and the throat closes.

units: the practitioner opens the session with a harmless question about meals
the young lad claims that he cannot remember
the young lad shuts himself off and folds his arms
the practitioner shifts the subject and speaks of the sound of the rain
the young lad owns up to dreading meals with the family
he explains that everyone at the table stares at him
the practitioner asks him which seat he would rather have
he points to the end of the table, next to the doorway
the practitioner suggests that he raise the matter at home
he agrees in the end and says that he will come back
text: The session opened on a question that seemed to lead absolutely nowhere: the psychologist asked the lad what he had eaten the evening before. He said he could not remember, then turned sullen and silent, arms folded hard across his chest. She did not press him for anything more. She talked instead about the rain hitting the glass and the colour of the sky. After a while the boy said that meals with the family unsettled him, because everyone there watched him without let-up. She asked him what he would do if the seat were his to choose. He said he would take the end of the table, right by the door. She suggested he raise it at home, in words of his own choosing. He wavered, then agreed. On his way out he called back that he would return, and he smiled without turning round.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of long ago put the states of the soul down to inner liquids
that theory won people over because it offered a workable remedy
low spirits were treated by diet or by drawing off blood
failure repeated again and again weakened the belief
watching things directly took the place of the theory
healers recorded the same signs for fear and for rage
they tied those states to the nerves rather than to a fluid
suffering of the mind stopped being seen as a taint to be driven out
out of that reversal came the idea that speech listened to can cure
text: Long before measurement took hold, healers put the states of the soul down to inner liquids that had to be brought back into balance. The doctrine held because it gave people something to do: if low spirits came of an excess, diet or the opening of a vein would surely draw it off. Failure after failure ate away at that confidence, and watching took over from doctrine. Physicians noticed that fear and fury threw up the same signs in patients who had nothing else in common, and they concluded that such states belonged to the nerves and not to any liquid. The consequence of that was a considerable one. Suffering of the mind stopped being handled as a taint to be flushed out, and began instead to be questioned. Out of that turn came the notion that speech carefully received could itself cure.

units: speaking in front of an audience quickens the heart and dampens the hands
the voice starts to shake in that situation
fear itself is not to blame, since it makes the body ready to act
the difficulty comes from the thoughts added on top of the fear
you expect to be shamed and you watch out for unfriendly faces
that watching pushes the alarm higher still
the first remedy is to make the out-breath longer than the in-breath
that lengthening quietens the beat of the heart
the second remedy is to put your attention on a willing listener
carrying your attention outwards breaks the circle that feeds itself
text: It has surely happened to you at some point. Just before you speak to a roomful of attentive people, the heart thumps, the palms turn damp and cold, and the voice starts to shake. Fear is not the trouble; fear is getting you ready to move. The trouble is what you pile on top of it. You tell yourself you are about to look a fool, you scan for the one hard face in the room, and the alarm climbs a notch. The way out comes down to two very ordinary moves. First, breathe out for longer than you breathe in; a stretched out-breath settles the heart. Second, attend to someone else rather than to yourself: find the most willing face in front of you and speak to that person. Turning your attention outwards cuts the loop that keeps you trapped. You may still shake, but you will get to the end.

units: two men have been waiting since the same hour for the same medical test
the first reads a magazine and speaks of his vegetable patch
the second checks the display board over and over
the second gets to his feet each time a name is called out
both men say they feel the same unease
the first tells himself that he will soon know something
the second expects the worst outcome
a nurse predicts that the second will come out worn down
the nurse reckons that a word can turn a wait right around
text: In the waiting area of a hospital treatment unit, two men have sat since the same hour, called in for the same examination. The first leafs through a magazine, his shoulders low; he says his mind is on his vegetable patch. The second, taut with worry, checks the display board at regular intervals and rises whenever a name sounds down the corridor. Both of them say they feel exactly the same apprehension. The difference lies elsewhere: one tells himself he will shortly know where he stands, the other tells himself he will shortly hear the worst. A nurse who has watched such pairings for a good many years remarks that the second will come out of it worn to the bone, while the first will come out merely relieved. A word, she adds, is sometimes enough to tip a wait from one side to the other.

units: you need a thin notebook and you keep it on you for a week
each evening you write three lines and no more
the first line names the feeling that ruled, with a precise word
vague words are set aside in favour of exact ones
the second line gives the part of the body where the feeling showed
the third line names the event that came before the feeling
you forbid yourself any rereading before the week is out
reading it back too soon bends the record out of shape
at the end you spread the pages out to spot what keeps returning
the exercise is repeated in the season that follows
text: Get hold of a slim notebook, the sort that slides into a pocket, and keep it on you for a full week. When evening comes, open it on your knees and set down three lines, not one more. On the first, name the feeling that ruled the day, using the truest word you can find: not bad, but tightness, or weariness, or lift. On the second, write where it lodged itself, whether the throat, the neck or the belly. On the third, name whatever came before it, even if the link looks thin to you. Read nothing back until the week is out; reading it too soon bends the record out of shape. On the last evening, lay the pages in front of you and look for what keeps returning. You will find regular patterns that memory alone could never have held. Then shut the notebook without judging it, and begin again next season.

units: a team of researchers ran a protocol in two similar hospital units
the first stage came down to measuring without stepping in
the measurements bore on the pulse and the sweating of the nursing staff
peaks were recorded at the moment of the spoken handover between teams
the second stage imposed a short break before every handover
the instruction asked for slower breathing during that break
the third stage set the records of the two units against each other
the unit given the break showed a better variability of the pulse
the authors remain careful because the loads of each team differ
text: A team of researchers began their protocol at the start of the cold season, in two comparable hospital units. The first phase went no further than recording: heart rate and sweating were logged in the nursing staff across their shifts, with nobody stepping in at any point. When it closed, the traces showed repeated peaks at the moment of the spoken handover. The second phase brought in a short compulsory pause before every handover, with an instruction to slow the breathing. The third phase set the readings of the two units side by side. The gap widened week by week: the team given the pause showed a more favourable heart rate variability, and damp hands turned up less often. The authors draw their conclusion carefully, since the units they followed do not carry loads of the same weight.
